<<EasyJet Soars Despite Brexit Turbulence>>

Section 1
EasyJet has reported a turbulent financial year, with profits tumbling 17% as the post-Brexit slump in the pound carved more than £100m from its bottom line. Despite this setback, the budget airline managed to fly a record 80.2 million passengers, nearly 10% more than the previous year, on planes that were fuller than ever. Revenues climbed past £5bn, but fares had to be trimmed to keep seats occupied in what chief executive Carolyn McCall described as "a difficult year for the aviation industry." The carrier's strategy of securing top positions at Europe's busiest hubs — towering above competitors like a tower of operational efficiency — has helped it weather a storm that has sunk several rival airlines into bankruptcy. McCall emphasised that friendly service and disciplined cost control remained the company's strategic anchors.

Section 2
Profits before tax fell from £494m to £408m, and although easyJet paid less in dollar terms for fuel, the weakness of sterling added £101m in additional costs. Brexit has also forced the airline to rethink its corporate structure, daring to confront a regulatory challenge that few in the aviation society have faced so directly. To ensure easyJet remains majority-owned and controlled by EU nationals after 2019, the company plans to ask shareholders at its 2018 AGM to approve powers that would compel UK investors to sell their stakes if necessary. Founder Stelios Haji-Ioannou, who holds dual UK-Cypriot nationality and owns roughly a third of the shares, will be classified as EU-owned, providing a substantial cushion. McCall dismissed concerns, calling the move "a technical, administrative thing."

Section 3
Investors responded warmly to the results, with shares rising more than 5% in early trading on the back of strong forward bookings and improved revenue in the new financial year. Analysts say the airline's resilience is no fluke; it has handled regulatory turbulence the way a seasoned angler might treat a fishing expedition in choppy waters — patient, prepared, and confident in the catch. With capacity leaving the market as weaker rivals collapse, easyJet appears poised to treat its shareholders to brighter skies ahead. While Brexit continues to cast long shadows over the European aviation industry, McCall's leadership suggests that easyJet intends not merely to survive the transition, but to emerge as one of the continent's defining carriers.
